parts.intro: You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman who works for a storage company and a man who wants to rent a storage unit.

turns.text: Good morning, Keystone Self Storage, Rachel speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hello. I'd like to rent a storage unit for a few months.
Of course. Could I have your name first?
Yes, it's Daniel Pelham.
Could you spell the surname for me, please?
Sure. It's P-E-L-H-A-M.
Thank you, Mr Pelham. And may I ask why you need the storage? It just helps us suggest the right kind of unit.

Well, originally I was planning to move abroad for work, so I thought I'd need somewhere for everything. But that's fallen through, actually. What's happening now is that our flat is being renovated, new kitchen, new floors, the lot, so everything has to come out for about three months.
I see. What size were you thinking of?
I thought 4 square metres might be enough, but my wife says that's far too small once you add the sofa and the wardrobe.
She's probably right. Four is quite tight for furniture.
Let's say 6 square metres, then. That should be plenty.
Fine. And what will you mainly be storing?
Furniture, mostly. The sofa, a wardrobe, a dining table and chairs. And then a lot of boxes of books. I've got hundreds of them, I'm afraid.
Got it. Now, when would you like the unit from?
The builders start on the 15th of March, so I'd want to move things in a few days before that. Could I have it from the 12th?
Let me check. Hmm, the 12th is a Sunday, and we don't sign up new customers on Sundays. How about the 14th?
The 14th is fine. That still gives me a day before the builders arrive.
Lovely. Now, the price. A unit that size is normally 65 pounds a month, but we have a special offer at the moment for anyone staying three months or more, so for you it would be 58 pounds a month.
58. That's better than I expected.
That doesn't include insurance, though. That's an extra 4 pounds a month, and it's compulsory unless you have your own policy that covers storage.
I'll take yours, I think. And how do I get in? Do I collect a key?
No, there are no keys. You'll be given a personal code, and you enter it on the keypad at the gate. The site is open from six in the morning until ten at night, every day of the week.
That's good, because I'll probably be coming after work.
When you come in to sign the contract, you'll need to bring some photo identification, a passport or a driving licence, and also proof of address, so a recent bank statement or a utility bill.
Proof of address. Okay, I'll find a bill.
You'll also need a lock for the door of your unit. You can buy one of ours for 8 pounds, or bring your own if it's a strong one.
I've got a really good padlock at home already, so I'll use that.
That's fine. Do you need any packing materials?
What do you have?
We sell a pack of ten strong cardboard boxes for 12 pounds.
Yes, I'll have a pack of those. I don't have nearly enough for all the books. Oh, and I'll need a trolley to move the heavy things in. Is there a charge for that?
No, the trolleys are free to use. They're by the lift.
Brilliant. And how do I pay? Should I bring cash when I come in?
Actually, we don't accept cash any more. You can set up a direct debit when you sign, but most of our customers find it easiest to pay by card on our website before they arrive.
I'll do it online, then.
Perfect. I'll email you the link now.

parts.intro: You will hear a woman from a walking organisation talking on a local radio programme about a new coastal walking trail.

turns.text: Good morning and welcome back to Coastline Weekend. With me in the studio is Lena Marsh from the Southern Shores Walking Trust, who's here to tell us about the new coastal trail opening next month. Welcome, Lena.

Thanks for having me. Well, it's been a long time coming. The Bluewater Coast Trail, as we're calling it, joins up a lot of older paths that used to stop and start, so for the first time you can walk all the way from the harbour at Port Ellery to Wickett Cove without going onto a main road. People often assume it's a short day walk. When we first drew up the plans, it was going to be about 32 kilometres, but we managed to add the headland section, so the final length is 46 kilometres. Most people will do it over three days, although some very fit walkers on our test days managed it in two.

I'm often asked who paid for it all. A lot of people think it was the local council, and they did help by arranging access to private land, but the bulk of the money, around eighty percent, came from a conservation charity, the Harlow Foundation. The rest was raised by local businesses, mainly cafes and guesthouses who'll benefit from more visitors.

Now, you won't get lost. We did think about painted arrows on the rocks, but the rangers felt that would spoil the landscape. And metal signs rust very quickly by the sea. So instead there are short wooden posts, every five hundred metres or so, with a small wave symbol carved into the top. They're easy to spot once you know what you're looking for.

The one thing I really want to stress is the tides. A couple of sections cross beaches that are completely underwater at high tide, so please check the tide times before you set out each morning. There are inland routes you can take instead, but they add quite a lot of distance. And you don't need to book anything. The shelters along the way are first come, first served.

The official opening is on Saturday the 9th. There was talk of holding a fun run, but we decided that didn't really suit the idea of a slow, peaceful walk. So instead there'll be guided walks led by our rangers during the day, and then in the evening a concert of local folk music down at the harbour.

Let me take you quickly through the main sections, heading from west to east. The first stretch goes round Gullhaven Bay. It's very gentle, flat sand mostly, and at low tide there are wonderful rock pools that children love to explore, so allow extra time if you've got kids with you.

Next comes Marrow Point, the headland section I mentioned. There used to be a lighthouse out on the point, but it was knocked down in a storm many years ago. What's left of it has been made safe, and the ruins are a lovely spot to stop and look out to sea. We had planned to put picnic tables there too, but the wind is so strong that they'd simply blow away, so just bring something to sit on.

Then you reach Tern Cliffs. This is the toughest part of the whole trail. There are around three hundred steep steps cut into the cliff face, so take your time and don't try it in wet weather. Some people expect to see lots of seabirds nesting on the cliffs, and you might see a few, but for proper birdwatching you'll want the next section.
That's Saltbrook Estuary, where the river meets the sea. We've built a wooden bird hide there, looking out over the mudflats, and in spring and autumn it's full of wading birds.

And finally there's Wickett Cove, where the trail ends. There's a small cafe run by the local surf club, which is the perfect place to celebrate finishing. Parking at the cove is very limited, though, so we'd recommend leaving your car at Port Ellery and taking the shuttle bus back.
That all sounds wonderful. Lena, thank you for joining us.

parts.intro: You will hear two engineering students, Priya and Tom, discussing their project on bamboo as a building material with their tutor.

turns.text: Come in, both of you, and sit down. So, this is our progress meeting for the materials project. Remind me where you've got to with the bamboo idea.

Well, when we first proposed it, we were going to look at bamboo scaffolding, because it's still used on high-rise building sites in some countries. But we found there's already a lot written on that, and most of it is about safety regulations rather than the material itself.

And I pushed for flooring for a while, but that turned out to be mainly about surface finishes. So in the end we've decided to focus on bamboo as the main structural material for low-rise housing, so one- and two-storey homes.
That sounds like a sensible scope. What's struck you most in the reading so far?

For me, well, I knew it was strong in tension. Some sources compare it to steel if you measure strength against weight, so that wasn't really a shock. And everyone knows it grows incredibly quickly. Some species put on almost a metre a day. What actually surprised me most was that despite growing so fast, a stem needs between three and five years to mature before it's any good for building. Cut it too early and it's weak.
Yes, that catches a lot of people out. Priya, what about you?

I was more interested in the problems. Everyone assumes the biggest one is fire, and it is a concern, but there are treatments that help a lot. Insects are another issue. But the engineers we read all seem to agree that the main difficulty is that every pole is different. The diameter and the wall thickness vary along the length and from one pole to the next, so it's really hard to design standard joints.
Exactly. Steel and concrete are predictable; bamboo isn't. Now, you did some testing in the lab, didn't you?
We did compression tests on twelve samples. Most behaved as we'd expected, but three of them split along the grain at quite low loads.
Any idea why?

We wondered at first whether they came from younger stems, but the supplier's records show they were all the same age, and they'd all been cut at the right time of year. We think the problem was that those three had been dried too quickly. The technician told us the oven setting had been wrong that week.
That's worth discussing in your report as a limitation, then. So what's your next step?
We were thinking of visiting a construction firm, but the nearest one that builds with bamboo is hours away.

I'd actually suggest something more useful. A former student of mine is now an architect, and she's designed several bamboo houses. Talking to her would give you the design perspective that's missing at the moment. I'll send you her email address.
That would be great, thank you.
Right, let's go through your draft report section by section. First, the history of bamboo construction. It's interesting, but it's six pages long.
I did wonder whether we should just take it out completely.
No, I wouldn't remove it. It gives the reader useful context. But do cut it down to a page or so.
Okay. Then there's the section with our test results.
Those are the heart of the project. But twelve samples really isn't enough to draw firm conclusions. Could you test some more?
The lab has free time next month, so we could do another twenty.
Good. Do that, and add the new results to the section.
Then the cost comparison with timber and concrete. We've got several pages of tables there.
The figures are important, but all those tables break up your argument. Put them at the back, in an appendix, and just summarise the main figures in the text.
And the case study of the community hall?
We weren't sure about that one.
Honestly, that's the best part of the whole report. It's clear and well organised. Leave it exactly as it is.
Finally, there's the section on protecting bamboo from insects. It's a bit thin.
It's short because many of the same chemicals are used against fire as well. Why not put it together with your section on fire treatment, so you have one section on treatments?
That makes a lot of sense. We'll do that.

parts.intro: You will hear part of a biology lecture about how migrating birds sleep.

turns.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're turning to a question that puzzled biologists for a very long time: how do birds that migrate over huge distances manage to sleep? Some species cross oceans or deserts where there's simply nowhere safe to land, and a few may stay in the air for days or even weeks at a time. For years the assumption was that they must somehow do without sleep altogether, which always seemed unlikely, since losing sleep has serious effects on almost every animal we've studied.

Part of the answer lies in something called unihemispheric sleep. This means that one half, or hemisphere, of the brain sleeps while the other half remains awake. Interestingly, you can often tell which half is asleep just by looking at the bird, because the eye connected to the waking hemisphere stays open, while the other eye closes.

This was first studied not in migrating birds at all, but in ducks resting on the ground. Researchers noticed that when ducks slept in a row, the birds at the two ends of the row were far more likely to sleep with one eye open, and that eye was almost always the one facing away from the group, in other words towards the direction a predator might come from. The ducks in the middle, protected by their neighbours, tended to sleep with both eyes shut.

Now, watching ducks on a pond is one thing, but measuring sleep in a bird flying over the ocean is quite another. The breakthrough came when engineers produced recording devices light enough to be carried in flight. These are attached to the bird's head, and they record the electrical activity of the brain, while a separate sensor tracks the bird's movements. In one well-known study, researchers fitted these devices to large seabirds that spend several days at sea looking for food, and then recovered them when the birds returned to their nests.

The results were striking in two ways. First, the birds did sleep in flight, sometimes with both hemispheres at once, which nobody had predicted. But they slept remarkably little: on average around 40 minutes per day in the air, compared with more than 12 hours a day once they were back on land. Second, the sleep happened mostly while the birds were gliding upwards in circles on rising currents of warm air, rather than while they were flapping, and almost all of it occurred after dark. The individual episodes of sleep were also very short, lasting only a few seconds each, although there might be hundreds of them in a single night.

What about smaller birds, such as songbirds, which usually migrate at night and rest during the day? Here much of the evidence comes from laboratory work. During the migration season, caged songbirds become extremely active at night, hopping and fluttering around. This restlessness appears even when the birds cannot see the sky, which tells us that it's driven by an internal clock rather than by outside signals. Naturally, these birds get much less sleep than usual during this period. Yet in experiments where they had been trained to do simple tasks, such as pecking a key to receive food, their performance stayed the same. By contrast, when the same birds were kept awake in a similar way outside the migration season, they made far more mistakes. So it seems that during migration these birds somehow become resistant to the normal effects of sleep loss.

That isn't the whole story, though. Migrants also make up for lost sleep during stopovers, the days they spend on the ground feeding between flights. Observations show that they take many short naps during the day, often in a typical position with the head turned backwards and the beak tucked into the feathers on the back. This position seems to help them save heat, which matters because they're also trying to build up fat reserves as fast as possible.

Why does any of this matter beyond biology? Well, if we could understand how these birds resist the effects of sleep loss, it might one day help people whose work involves long periods without proper rest, for example pilots on long-distance flights, or doctors working night shifts. We're a long way from that, but it's one reason this research attracts funding.

Finally, a point about conservation. Migrating birds rely on darkness both to find their way and to rest, and artificial light from cities can confuse them, draw them off course and disturb their sleep at stopover sites. Some cities have started switching off decorative lighting on tall buildings during the busiest weeks of migration, and early results suggest this reduces the number of birds that crash into buildings. Next week we'll look at how birds navigate.

passages.title: The Long Road to the Modern Bicycle
passages.text:
Few machines have changed everyday life as quietly as the bicycle. Today it is so familiar that it is easy to assume it was invented in a single moment of inspiration. In fact, the machine that most people now ride took almost eighty years to emerge, through a long series of experiments, false starts and passing fashions in Europe and North America during the nineteenth century.

The earliest ancestor of the bicycle is usually said to be the "running machine", demonstrated in 1817 by a forestry inspector in a small German state. It consisted of two wooden wheels placed one behind the other and joined by a wooden frame. The rider sat astride the frame and pushed against the ground with his feet, rather like a child on a modern balance bike. There were no pedals at all. On a good road the machine could reach around 13 kilometres per hour, and its inventor promoted it as a cheaper alternative to the horse, partly because a series of poor harvests had made feeding horses very expensive. For a short time running machines became a fashion among wealthy young men in London and Paris, where they were nicknamed "hobby horses". The enthusiasm faded within two years, however. Riders tended to use the smooth pavements to avoid rutted roads, injuring pedestrians, and several cities banned the machines altogether.

For the next forty years, inventors searched for a way of driving the wheels without touching the ground. A number of three- and four-wheeled vehicles were built, powered by hand levers or foot treadles, but most were heavy and slow. One account claims that a village blacksmith in Scotland built a two-wheeled machine driven by levers around 1839, but the evidence for this rests largely on stories written down decades later, and historians remain divided over whether it ever existed.

The real breakthrough came in Paris in the 1860s, when pedals and cranks were attached directly to the hub of the front wheel. The resulting machine, known as the velocipede, had an iron frame and wooden wheels with iron tyres. In English it quickly earned the nickname "boneshaker", because on the cobbled streets of the time it transmitted every bump straight to the rider. Even so, it caused a sensation. By 1868 a single Paris workshop was producing several hundred machines a year, riding schools opened in a number of cities, and the first organised races were held. Yet the velocipede weighed around 30 kilograms, and the craze had largely passed by the early 1870s.

Because the pedals were fixed to the front wheel, one turn of the pedals produced exactly one turn of the wheel. The only way to travel further with each turn was to make the front wheel bigger, and that is precisely what manufacturers did. The result was the high-wheeler of the 1870s and 1880s, with a front wheel that could measure up to one and a half metres across and a tiny wheel behind. Two innovations made these machines lighter and faster than the velocipede: solid rubber tyres, and thin wheels built with spokes of tightly stretched wire rather than wood. High-wheelers were popular with athletic young men, who formed clubs and undertook remarkable long-distance tours. But they were also dangerous. The rider sat high above the front wheel, so that any sudden stop, caused by a stone or a pothole, could throw him forward over the handlebars, an accident known as "taking a header". Older people were largely excluded, and for women, whose long skirts made climbing onto the machine almost impossible, the high-wheeler was hardly an option at all.

Manufacturers therefore experimented with designs they advertised as "safety" machines. The solution that eventually won was to drive the rear wheel by means of a chain. Through a large front gear and a small rear one, a chain allowed a wheel of ordinary size to turn quickly, so there was no longer any need for an enormous front wheel. The safety bicycle of the mid-1880s had two wheels of similar size, and the rider sat between them, low enough to put both feet on the ground. At first, many high-wheel enthusiasts ridiculed the new machines as slow and unmanly, but within a few years safety bicycles were winning races against them. A further improvement followed in 1888, when a veterinary surgeon developed an air-filled tyre for his young son's tricycle. Pneumatic tyres made riding far more comfortable as well as faster, and within five years they had been fitted to almost every new bicycle.

By the 1890s the diamond-shaped frame made of steel tubes had become standard, and the bicycle had taken more or less its modern form. A boom followed. As factories adopted mass-production methods borrowed from the sewing machine and arms industries, prices fell sharply, and by the end of the decade a new bicycle cost a skilled worker a few weeks' wages rather than several months'. The social effects were considerable. Cycling gave many women a new degree of independence and encouraged lighter, more practical clothing, while cyclists' associations campaigned for better roads years before motor cars became common. Many of the techniques developed for bicycles, from ball bearings to light steel tubing, were later used by the builders of the first cars and aeroplanes.

passages.title: Mangrove Forests: Living Defences of the Coast
passages.text:
A  Along tropical and subtropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea, grow some of the most unusual forests on the planet. Mangroves are trees and shrubs that live in the zone between low and high tide, rooted in soft mud that is flooded with salt water twice a day. They are found on the coasts of around 120 countries, mostly between latitudes 30 degrees north and south of the equator, and together they cover roughly 140,000 square kilometres, an area smaller than many people imagine and one that has shrunk considerably over the past half-century. The largest continuous stretches lie in South and Southeast Asia, but extensive forests also line parts of West Africa, Central America and northern Australia.

B  Few plants could tolerate the conditions in which mangroves thrive. Salt water would kill most trees, but mangroves deal with it in several ways: some species filter salt out at the roots, while others take it in and then push it out through special glands on their leaves, where it can sometimes be seen as white crystals. A second challenge is the mud itself, which is so waterlogged that it contains almost no oxygen. To overcome this, many mangroves send up vertical roots, like pencils sticking out of the mud, which have tiny pores through which air can pass down to the buried root system. Others are supported by arching stilt roots that hold the trunk above the water, giving the forest its characteristic tangled appearance.

C  It is this tangle of roots and trunks that makes mangroves valuable as coastal defences. When waves enter a mangrove forest, they lose energy as the water is forced around countless obstacles. Field measurements suggest that wave height can fall by between a third and a half over the first 100 metres of forest. The most important factor, researchers have found, is not the species or the age of the trees but simply the width of the forest belt: a narrow fringe a few dozen metres deep offers modest protection, while a belt several kilometres wide can significantly reduce the inland flooding caused by storm surges. Even so, no forest can entirely stop the largest surges, and scientists warn against presenting mangroves as a guarantee of safety.

D  Mangroves also shape the land itself. Their roots slow the movement of water, so that fine particles of mud and sand carried by rivers and tides settle among them. Over time this sediment, together with decaying leaves and roots, can raise the level of the forest floor. Where there is a good supply of sediment, this process allows mangroves to keep pace with a moderate rise in sea level; where dams upstream have reduced the flow of sediment, however, the forests are far more likely to be drowned. The same waterlogged soils also lock away large amounts of carbon, because dead plant material decays very slowly without oxygen. Per hectare, mangroves can store several times more carbon than most tropical forests on dry land.

E  The economic case for protecting mangroves has become clearer in recent years. A study of the Pelora delta compared three ways of defending a stretch of low-lying farmland: a concrete sea wall, a restored mangrove belt, and a combination of a lower sea wall with mangroves planted in front of it. The sea wall alone was the most expensive option to build and maintain, partly because waves striking it directly caused constant damage. Mangroves alone were the cheapest, but they did not provide enough protection during the strongest storms. The combined approach proved the most cost-effective over a 30-year period, since the trees absorbed much of the wave energy before it reached the wall, which could therefore be built lower and repaired less often.

F  Despite such findings, mangroves continue to be cleared, mainly to make way for shrimp farms, rice fields and coastal development. Replanting has become popular with governments and charities, but the results have often been disappointing. In one large programme more than a million seedlings were planted, yet a survey five years later found that fewer than one in five had survived. The main reason was that many had been planted on open mudflats below the natural mangrove zone, where they were covered by water for too long each day. Others were placed in abandoned shrimp ponds whose walls still blocked the natural flow of the tides. Ecologists now argue that restoring the flow of water and allowing seeds to arrive naturally often works better than planting.

G  Increasingly, the most successful projects are those that involve the people who live beside the forests. In several regions, legal responsibility for managing mangroves has been transferred from national agencies to village committees. Their members patrol the forest, agree rules on the harvesting of firewood and decide which areas should be left untouched. In return, they earn an income from sustainable activities such as crab fishing and small-scale ecotourism. Where such arrangements are supported by clear land rights and a fair sharing of income, mangrove cover has stabilised or even increased.

passages.title: Should Governments Measure Happiness?
passages.text:
Over the past two decades, a growing number of governments have begun to collect data not only on income, employment and health, but also on how satisfied their citizens are with their lives. National statistics offices now routinely ask large samples of the population to rate, on a scale from 0 to 10, how satisfied they are with their lives nowadays, how happy they felt yesterday, and whether the things they do are worthwhile. Enthusiasts argue that such figures should sit alongside, or even replace, gross domestic product (GDP) as the main measure of a nation's progress. Critics regard the whole exercise as at best a distraction and at worst a threat to personal freedom. In my view, both camps overstate their case.

The enthusiasts' argument begins with the weaknesses of GDP. It measures market activity, not well-being: it rises when money is spent rebuilding towns after a flood, and it counts the sale of products that damage health just as it counts those that improve it. Life-satisfaction surveys, by contrast, attempt to capture what people actually value. They have produced some striking findings. Losing a job, for example, appears to reduce well-being far more than the loss of income alone would predict, while loneliness and long journeys to work turn out to matter a great deal. Such findings, the enthusiasts say, should change how public money is spent. I find this argument persuasive up to a point. GDP was never designed as a measure of welfare, and its own creators warned against using it in that way.

Critics usually respond that happiness is too subjective to be measured. This objection, however, is weaker than it first appears. People's answers to well-being questions are related to things we would expect: they agree reasonably well with ratings given by friends and family, with how often people smile, and even with later health outcomes. The measures are not perfect, but neither are the official figures for unemployment or inflation, which involve many judgement calls of their own. A more serious problem is one of scale. Even if the question stays the same, people's standards may change. As a society becomes richer, its members may quietly adjust what they mean by a "7". This may explain why average life satisfaction in several wealthy countries has hardly moved in fifty years despite large increases in income. It does not necessarily mean that nothing has improved; it may simply mean that the ruler has stretched.

The real danger lies not in measurement but in the temptation to turn a single well-being figure into a target. It is a familiar rule of public administration that a measure ceases to be useful once people are rewarded for changing it. A government judged on national happiness scores might be tempted to improve them in ways that have little to do with people's lives, by encouraging lower expectations, perhaps, or by public campaigns reminding citizens how fortunate they are. This is not merely a theoretical risk. When the regional government of Valdoria linked part of the funding for its town councils to local life-satisfaction scores, the scores duly rose, but independent inspections found no improvement in the services the councils provided. Several councils, it emerged, had simply arranged for their surveys to take place during local festivals.

Where well-being data is most valuable, I would argue, is not in setting national targets but in comparing particular policies. Because the effects of very different programmes can be expressed in the same unit, changes in life satisfaction, it becomes possible to ask whether a given sum would do more good if spent on a new park, a hospital ward or a training scheme for the unemployed. Several analyses of this kind have suggested that treatment for common mental illnesses produces far more well-being per unit of money than many transport projects. Even here, though, caution is needed. Such analysis naturally favours policies whose effects appear quickly and are easy to capture in a survey. The benefits of early childhood education, for instance, may not be fully visible for decades, and a method that overlooks them could lead governments seriously astray.

What, then, of the claim that it is simply not the business of the state to make people happy? I have some sympathy with the instinct behind it, but I think it is misplaced. Governments already make countless decisions that affect well-being, from planning permission for housing to the opening hours of public libraries. The question is not whether they influence happiness, but whether they do so with or without evidence. To ignore the evidence is not a neutral position; it is merely a less informed one. What matters is that the data informs decisions rather than dictates them, and that citizens remain free to pursue their own idea of a good life.

Measuring happiness, in short, is neither a revolution nor a fraud. It is a useful additional instrument, best used modestly, as one dial on the dashboard among many. The greatest risk is not that governments will measure happiness, but that they will come to trust the measurement more than it deserves.
